Three stars hang in the sky above Seizan. Amaterasu burns gold. Susanoo burns blue-white. Tsukuyomi burns red.
The trees of the Seidōrin Mori grow with bark of burnished copper-bronze that catches sunlight like armour.
Sei — the magic that flows through all living things — vanished completely for over three thousand years. No one alive remembers why.
Unlicensed logging in the Bronze Wood Forest is a capital offence. The clans do not negotiate on this.
Four moons circle Seizan. Sailors call them the Sisters' Tears, and plan their voyages around them.
The Emperor has been dead for five years. No successor has been confirmed. The throne sits empty.
During Tatsunami season, the four moons align and the ocean rises. Coastal villages evacuate as a matter of routine.
The Hoshimori Plateau sits so high above the clouds that stars are visibly brighter there than anywhere else in the archipelago.
Ronin — samurai without masters — are at an all-time high. The political vacuum has left thousands unsworn.
The Serenia-kai is a vast inland sea whose surface shifts colour with the seasons. Its tides are governed by four moons, and its shoreline can retreat hundreds of metres without warning.
Honour is not abstract in Kagekuni. It is a currency, a weapon, and a sentence.
The leaves of the Bronze Wood shed entirely in a single night when the temperature drops below a certain threshold. By morning, the forest floor gleams like a smithy.

Kanedōchiri — the Bronze-Fall — is the festival of the Seidōrin's single-night shedding. Villages along the forest hang lanterns in the canopy as the cold draws near; the first leaf to fall is kept by the eldest priest and held in trust until the next year.
Seven dragon clans ruled Kagekuni before the first human emperor rose to power.
Grass grows in deep violet across the open plains of Kusa. The wind moving through it produces sounds that some mistake for voices.
The Kinryūgawa — the Gold Dragon River — runs faintly gold at dawn. The fish that swim in it are called kinuo, and their meat commands a premium in Heian.
Province Sora borders nearly every other province in Hokori. It is also the least populated and most dangerous to cross.
The First Golden Age lasted over four thousand years. Eight emperors reigned. Then the magic disappeared.
Rivers in Kagekuni run faintly luminescent at night. No one considers this unusual.
Kurogane Yama — Black Iron Mountain — dominates southern Tsuchi. The mountains around it are old, weathered, and rich with ore.
Highland fog sometimes carries the scent of incense, though no shrine is near. The old guides warn against following it — those who do, they say, return changed if they return at all.
The Great Granaries of Tsuchimoto hold enough grain to feed Hokori through two years of failed harvests.
The constellations above Kagekuni do not match any star chart from the world beyond. Navigators learn a different sky.
Enshiyama, the third highest peak on Hokori, rises from the northern end of the island. It is an active volcano whose crater lake glows faintly orange at night.
Sound behaves strangely beneath the canopy of the Bronze Wood. Conversations carry too far or not at all.

The Emperor's Highway extends from Heian in three directions, and its licensed sea routes carry the imperial banner to the outer islands. Everything important in Hokori is measured by distance along it.
Social hierarchy in Kagekuni is not a suggestion. Emperor, daimyō, samurai, merchant, peasant — each rank carries weight the law enforces.
During the Dark Ages, the population of the archipelago fell by nearly half. Entire cities were abandoned to silence and weather.
The Eastern Lighthouse Chain along Nami's coast stretches for miles. Some of the stone foundations predate recorded history.
Seimasters study magic the way a scholar studies astronomy — with discipline, notation, and deep patience.
The Yōsei Mori — the Forest of Spirits — resists navigation. Compasses drift. Trails rearrange. The creatures within are unnervingly intelligent.
The Honogawa, the Flame River of Hi province, runs warm enough to scald in its upper reaches.
Talents — individuals born with innate magical ability — began appearing roughly a thousand years ago. They were hunted before they were understood.
There are two great alliances dividing Hokori: the Arashi in the north and west, and the Genso in the east and south. Three clans remain stubbornly independent.
The Obsidian Fields of Kurosō are vast plains of volcanic glass. Blades forged from it are prized across the archipelago.

Farmers in lowland Tsuchi say their ploughs catch on stonework beneath the fields — an old road, they reckon, though no one has dug far enough to be sure, and the elders disagree on where it might lead.
The Stormwatch Cliffs in Nami are the highest sea cliffs on Hokori. On clear days, the island of Kawa is visible from the edge.
Nami's buildings are constructed low and heavy, walls thick, roofs angled against the prevailing wind. Architecture here is a survival strategy.
Fishermen at Umigakure swear the Tidal Caves breathe. On the deepest low tides, they say, a wind comes out of them that has travelled further than any cave should reach.
In the year 16742, open war began between the Arashi and Genso alliances. Hokori has not known peace since.

The Kōri-no-Mori — the Ice Forest — occupies the northern shores of Mizu. Ancient trees grow intermixed with crystal trees whose trunks chime faintly in the wind. It is cold, old, and largely unexplored.
Clan Gekkō of Kaze province has gone silent. Their daimyō has not been seen publicly in some time, and the province has stopped communicating with the capital.

The Shadowfen Bridge near Sakura Mura is said to demand an honest secret from those who cross. The old folk swear that liars step onto the far bank and find themselves somewhere they never meant to be.
Three Golden Age observatories still stand on the Hoshimori Plateau, their bronze instruments oriented to alignments no living seimaster fully understands.
Minato-jō in the northwest and Namigashira in the northeast are the two great ports of Hokori. Most of what moves by sea passes through one of them.
Mountain passes through Sora are impassable in winter. Entire communities on either side are cut off for months.
The people of Hi province live beside an active volcano. Their humour is dry, their preparations thorough, and their patience for outsiders limited.
Religion in Kagekuni is animistic. Spirits dwell in rivers, mountains, and ancient trees. Shrines mark their resting places.
Kuroyami no Akuma — once called Takeda no Arata — found a necromantic tome on the island of Yūrei and raised an army of the dead. He was defeated. Some say the defeat was only temporary.
Magic officially returned to the world in the year 16687. They call it the Great Awakening, and the daimyō have been recruiting mages ever since.

Old roadside shrines still stand along forgotten paths. Travellers who leave a coin and a courtesy find their road easier; those who pass without acknowledgement, the old folk warn, find themselves taking longer than the map allows.
